thread.text: Three years afterward Jason sent Menelaus, the aforesaid Simon’s brother, to bear the money unto the king, and to put him in mind of certain necessary matters.

classes.title: From Brother To Betrayer

precepts.label: Job 34:11
precepts.why:
“Then Jason, who had undermined his own brother, being undermined by another, was compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Jason undermined his own brother Onias to become high priest, and then he got undermined by Menelaus, the brother of Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin. Now the high priest is of the tribe of Benjamin. You can't make this stuff up.

That is why Job 34:11 is here: “For the work of a man shall he render unto him, and cause every man to find according to his ways.” Whatever you do is going to come back on you. However you deal in this earth with your brother, with your neighbor, it is going to come back on you.

Jason sent Menelaus to bear the money to the king, and Menelaus flattered the king and “got the priesthood to himself, offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver.” Jason found the same thing he had done to his brother, and had to run. And later in the history the same thing comes back again on Jason and on Menelaus both: all that evil comes back on them.

precepts.label: Colossians 3:25
precepts.why:
Here is an easier verse to say what Job 34:11 says: “But he that doeth wrong shall receive for the wrong which he hath done: and there is no respect of persons.” You see how God gets down. In the world they call that karma. The Bible says if you do wrong, you shall receive for the wrong you have done.

There is no respect of persons. Jason was the high priest and it did not protect him: he undermined his own brother and was undermined by another. Andronicus was a man in authority, the king's deputy, and it did not protect him either. He came to Onias in deceit, gave him his right hand with oaths, drew him out of the sanctuary and killed him, and the king took away his purple, rent off his clothes, led him through the whole city “unto that very place, where he had committed impiety against Onias, there slew he the cursed murderer. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved.” He received for the wrong he had done, in the very place he did it.

precepts.label: Galatians 6:7
precepts.why:
“Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.” Don't be deceived, brothers and sisters. God is not mocked. Whatsoever you do in this earth, you are going to reap from what you have done.

So if you decide, I'm going to undermine my brother next to me, I'm going to do some deceitful stuff to my sister, it is going to come back to you. It might not be this year; it might be next year, but it is going to come.

That is the history of 2 Maccabees 4. Jason sowed undermining against his own brother and reaped being undermined by another, “compelled to flee into the country of the Ammonites.” Menelaus got the principality by flattery and money and went on to steal vessels of gold out of the temple, and Andronicus sowed deceit and murder against Onias and reaped death in that very place. Brothers turning on brothers for position all reap what they sow.

precepts.label: Ecclesiasticus 28:7-15
precepts.why:
When Onias found out Menelaus was stealing vessels of gold out of the temple, he reproved him and had to run for his life, fleeing from Jerusalem up to the sanctuary at Daphne by Antiochia in Syria. Sirach shows what drives a man like that from his place.

“Remember the commandments, and bear no malice to thy neighbour: remember the covenant of the Highest, and wink at ignorance.” Sometimes brothers and sisters may do something simple. Wink at it. It doesn't always have to be a counsel for small matters. “Abstain from strife, and thou shalt diminish thy sins: for a furious man will kindle strife”, and “A sinful man disquieteth friends, and maketh debate among them that be at peace.”

“An hasty contention kindleth a fire: and an hasty fighting sheddeth blood. If thou blow the spark, it shall burn: if thou spit upon it, it shall be quenched: and both these come out of thy mouth.” Your mouth has the power: you can blow on that spark and it will burn, or you can spit on it, let it go, and quench it.

“Curse the whisperer and doubletongued: for such have destroyed many that were at peace. A backbiting tongue hath disquieted many, and driven them from nation to nation”. We just read that Onias had to flee from Jerusalem up to Syria. “strong cities hath it pulled down, and overthrown the houses of great men.” A backbiting tongue overthrew the house of a great man, Onias, the real high priest.

precepts.label: 1 Timothy 3:7
precepts.why:
When Onias was murdered, “not only the Jews, but many also of other nations, took great indignation, and were much grieved for the unjust murder of the man”, and even Antiochus “was heartily sorry, and moved to pity, and wept, because of the sober and modest behaviour of him that was dead.” The white man was crying for Onias, because other nations respected Onias III.

That is his character. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations, and he was not trying to join with the other nations; he said, I'm not joining with you. But he still had a good report among them. “Moreover he must have a good report of them which are without; lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the devil.”

“Without” means without the truth. You must have a good report outside this truth. If we are at camp one day and somebody tries to do a drive-by on us because of something you did or said, what the hell is going on here? You have to have a good report within and without, like Onias.

precepts.label: 1 Thessalonians 4:12
precepts.why:
Somebody might say a good report with them that are without is only for somebody that desires the office of a bishop. No: “That ye may walk honestly toward them that are without, and that ye may have lack of nothing.”

You have to walk honestly toward them that are without the truth. You can't be outside the school, outside this truth, robbing, stealing, lying, using drugs, whatever little secret things you have going on.

Why “lack of nothing”? Because people are going to look out for you out there in the world. They are going to say, now this is a good dude, this is a good sister right here. That is what Onias had: a sober and modest behaviour that even the other nations honored, so that when he was slain without cause, they complained with the Jews.

precepts.label: Colossians 4:5
precepts.why:
“Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.” Walk in wisdom toward them that are without the truth, that don't know the truth.

“Redeeming the time” means be aware of the time you are in.

It goes with the good report of Onias. He had a good report among the Jews and among the other nations without joining himself to the other nations, and when he was unjustly murdered, the Jews and “certain of the Greeks that abhorred the fact also” complained because he “was slain without cause.” That is walking in wisdom toward them that are without: keeping yourself apart from their ways, and still carrying yourself so that they know you are righteous.

precepts.label: 1 Peter 2:12
precepts.why:
“Having your conversation honest among the Gentiles: that, whereas they speak against you as evildoers, they may by your good works, which they shall behold, glorify God in the day of visitation.”

They may speak against us as evildoers, but they shall behold our good works. Why would they glorify God? Because our people who are living like Gentiles will repent based on your conduct out there in the world.

That is the lesson of Onias in 2 Maccabees 4. His conduct was honest before the nations, and even the Greeks and the king wept for him. Menelaus and Andronicus dealt in flattery, theft and deceit, and they brought reproach. Our conversation outside this truth is how our own people living like Gentiles will see it and come to repentance.

precepts.label: Matthew 18:6
precepts.why:
When a false rumour went out that Antiochus was dead, Jason took a thousand men and assaulted the city. “But Jason slew his own citizens without mercy, not considering that to get the day of them of his own nation would be a most unhappy day for him; but thinking they had been his enemies, and not his countrymen.” He despised his own people.

“Howbeit for all this he obtained not the principality, but at the last received shame for the reward of his treason.” You think you can be a traitor and be honored and respected? No. Nobody likes a traitor. Even in Rise of the Planet of the Apes, the whole movie is about black people, they spray painted the word donkey on the traitor apes. That is the brothers who were in here in 2018, and some of the brothers who just bugged out in LA. You cannot be trusted.

Christ spoke of what it is to harm his own: “But whoso shall offend one of these little ones which believe in me, it were better for him that a millstone were hanged about his neck, and that he were drowned in the depth of the sea.” It would be better for the betrayer to have a millstone hanged about his neck and be drowned.

Jason offended and slew those who belonged to the Lord, and he got his reward: shame, fleeing from city to city, and dying in a strange land.

precepts.label: Matthew 26:24
precepts.why:
Jason “received shame for the reward of his treason.” Christ spoke directly about the betrayer: “The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born.” Put that with the millstone about the neck, and both mean the same thing for the traitor: go die.

See how all the evil Jason did came back on him. “In the end therefore he had an unhappy return, being accused before Aretas the king of the Arabians, fleeing from city to city, pursued of all men, hated as a forsaker of the laws, and being had in abomination as an open enemy of his country and countrymen, he was cast out into Egypt.”

“Thus he that had driven many out of their country perished in a strange land, retiring to the Lacedemonians”, that is Sparta, “thinking there to find succour by reason of his kindred: And he that had cast out many unburied had none to mourn for him, nor any solemn funerals at all, nor sepulchre with his fathers.”

It had been good for that man if he had not been born. That is what the scripture says about the betrayer, whether it is Jason with Onias, Judas with Christ, or those who betray their brethren in this truth today.
